creative.title: Why Your Hand Pain Keeps Getting Worse.
creative.description:
I've been a musculoskeletal pain specialist for 22 years and if your hands have been getting stiffer, achier, and harder to use…

Then what I am about to share with you is going to OUTRAGE you.

My name is Dr. Sarah. Board-certified musculoskeletal pain specialist.

Twenty-two years treating chronic joint pain, osteoarthritis, and the kind of hand and finger pain that slowly steals your independence one small task at a time.

And I'm breaking ranks with my own profession to tell you this.

So let me tell you what happened with one of my patients because her story is going to open your eyes to how messed up this really is.

Her name was Linda. 58 years old.

For four straight years, she dealt with this.

Her fingers so stiff in the morning they curled up tightly and were hard to open. By lunchtime her knuckles were aching. By evening she could barely grip a kettle. She had been active her whole life, knitted jumpers for her grandchildren, gardened every weekend, opened every jar in the house without thinking, and suddenly she had the hands of someone twenty years older.

She came through my clinic. Multiple doctors. Her GP. A physiotherapist. A rheumatologist. Me, the pain specialist. Thousands of pounds in appointments, blood tests, X-rays, referrals.

And you know what every single one of us told her?

"Your bloods are normal. It's not rheumatoid."

"It's just osteoarthritis. Wear and tear. Normal for your age."

"Take ibuprofen."

"Wear compression gloves."

Wear compression gloves. This woman couldn't open a jar of horseradish and we were telling her to buy tighter gloves.

Then we put her on naproxen. Then Voltarol gel three times a day. Then cortisone injections into her finger joints.

You know what happened?

The naproxen gave her stomach cramps so bad she stopped eating breakfast. The Voltarol wore off in an hour. The cortisone worked for six weeks, then four, then barely two.

And her hands? Still stiff. Still aching. Still getting worse.

The treatments masked the pain. But the joints kept degrading. The stiffness kept spreading. The life kept shrinking.

I watched this woman do everything I told her, spend thousands of pounds, take my prescriptions, and get worse. Not better. Worse.

And I did not understand why.

Until an integrative pain researcher stopped me in my tracks at a conference and taught me more about stiff, aching hands in thirty minutes than I had learned in two decades of practice.

November 2023. Edinburgh. The British Pain Society annual meeting.

I was sitting at a table during a coffee break, trying to uncurl my own fingers around the cup without wincing. Because eighteen months earlier — right around the time I went through the menopause — my own hands had started stiffening. And nothing I had been prescribing to patients for twenty-two years was working on me either.

That is when I noticed him.

Dr. Michael Lin. Integrative pain and inflammation researcher. He'd been writing notes all morning. Picking up his coffee. Shaking hands with colleagues. His fingers moved the way fingers move when they have never once been thought about.

No stiffness. No swollen knuckles. No hesitation before gripping.

I walked over.

"Excuse me. At your age, after writing all morning, how are your hands not in bits?"

He smiled.

The kind of smile that knows something you don't.

Then he looked down at my hands.

He didn't need to ask what was wrong.

"Dr. Sarah, may I show you something?"

"It'll take thirty minutes."

"But it'll completely change the way you understand hand and finger pain."

He pulled out a notepad.

Then he wrote one sentence across the top:

Joint degeneration is a symptom, NOT the root cause.

I stared at the words.

Because for nearly two decades, I'd been taught to treat stiff, aching hands as a joint problem.

Mask the pain with anti-inflammatories.

Rub on topical gel.

Squeeze the swelling down with compression gloves.

Inject cortisone into the worst joints.

And when all of that fails, tell the patient it's something they'll have to learn to live with.

But nobody had explained why the joints were breaking down to begin with.

Then the doctor said something I'd never heard before.

"The question you should be asking isn't…"

"'How do I stop the pain in the hands?'"

"The real question should be…"

"'Why are the joints in her fingers and wrists breaking down faster than her body can repair them?'"

That sentence hit me like a brick.

Because every treatment I'd prescribed worked the same way.

Painkillers masked the pain signal.

Voltarol gel temporarily numbed the surface.

Compression gloves squeezed the swelling.

Cortisone injections temporarily suppressed the local inflammation.

But none of them addressed why the inflammation was there in the first place.

He drew a simple picture of a finger joint.

Then he drew tiny arrows flooding in around the cartilage.

"This is chronic low-grade inflammation," he said.

"After menopause, a woman's body loses oestrogen."

"Oestrogen is the body's most powerful natural anti-inflammatory."

"Losing it is like removing a brake."

"Without that brake, inflammatory signals begin flooding the joints — especially the small, delicate joints in the hands and fingers."

Then he tapped the drawing.

"The inflammation attacks the cartilage. The cartilage thins. The joints stiffen. The fingers curl. The grip goes. The pain gets worse."

"And every treatment you prescribe treats what happens AFTER the inflammation has already done its damage."

Then he drew a tap above the hand with water pouring down.

"That's like mopping up a flooded floor while the tap is still running."

"You're cleaning up the damage."

"Not turning off what's causing it."

I sat there thinking about every patient I'd put on naproxen.

Every patient I'd told to buy compression gloves.

Every patient I'd injected with cortisone.

Every patient I'd told there was nothing more I could do.

I'd been treating the damage after it happened.

I hadn't been helping the body turn down the inflammation that was causing the damage in the first place.

Then he said something else I'd never heard in medical school.

"As women get older — especially after menopause — the inflammation becomes harder for the body to shut off on its own."

"Without oestrogen's protective brake, it accumulates."

"And as the chronic inflammation builds up around the finger joints, the wrists, the surrounding tissue…"

"The joints degrade faster than the body can repair them."

"When you're younger, your body can usually manage the inflammation and maintain the joint."

"But after 50, that balance shifts."

"The inflammation makes the small joints in the hands more vulnerable to breakdown."

"That's why temporarily masking the pain isn't the same as supporting a healthy inflammatory response."

This was the missing piece.

Because joint degeneration wasn't the root cause.

It was the symptom.

And for many women over 50 with stiff, aching, swollen hands, chronic post-menopausal inflammation was the hidden problem nobody was talking about.

Then he turned the page.

"Fortunately, there's one little-known pressure point most women over 50 are missing in this conversation."

I leaned forward.

He said:

"There's a point that runs along the index finger down to the webbing between the thumb. Healers call it the Hegu point. LI-4."

"It's been documented for over four thousand years."

"The Yellow Emperor's texts describe it. Modern acupuncturists still use it. Memorial Sloan Kettering teaches it."

"For four thousand years, stimulating this one point on the hand has been used to help the body calm its own pain and inflammatory signals."

"And here's what makes it so relevant for hand pain specifically."

He tapped the drawing of the hand.

"The Hegu point is ON the hand. The pressure point that helps regulate inflammation sits in the exact same area as the joints that are being damaged by it."

This was the missing piece.

And once you understand what consistent stimulation at this pressure point does…

You may never look at painkillers, compression gloves, and cortisone injections the same way again.

Because this one pressure point helps support healthy circulation through the hands and fingers.

It helps support the body's own pain-regulation pathways.

It helps support a healthier inflammation response — helping the body turn down the chronic inflammatory signals that are driving the joint damage.

And ultimately, it helps support what every painkiller, gel, glove, and injection fails to do — address the inflammation itself, not just the pain it causes.

I'd been treating the damaged joints.

But I hadn't been supporting the system responsible for protecting them.

Every treatment I'd prescribed for twenty-two years worked downstream.

Not one of them addressed the chronic inflammation attacking the joints from the inside.

And here's what made my blood boil.

This pressure point has been documented for four thousand years. Acupuncturists use it every single day. Researchers have studied it in clinical settings across the world.

But the connection between this pressure point, chronic inflammation, and hand pain after menopause was almost never discussed in mainstream medicine.

A small British company has now designed a ring — a simple, beautiful ring with therapeutic magnets — that delivers gentle, consistent acupressure stimulation at the Hegu point.

You wear it on the hand that needs it most. Every day.

And instead of masking the pain signal or numbing the surface or squeezing the swelling or injecting cortisone that wears off in a fortnight…

It helps the body turn down the tap.

And here's what you need to understand about timing.

Chronic inflammation doesn't improve by being ignored.

After menopause, without oestrogen's protective brake, inflammatory signals continue flooding the joints.

And every month you wait is another month where that inflammation continues breaking down the cartilage you have left.

So if your fingers are stiff and curled up every morning…

If you can't open a jar without asking for help…

If you've had to give up knitting or gardening because your hands won't cooperate…

If you're dropping things you used to hold without thinking…

If your doctor has told you it's just something you'll have to live with…

You MUST address the inflammation. Not just mask the pain.

Tap the link below to discover how the EverCalm ring is helping thousands of women support happier, more comfortable hands — without pills, without injections, without being told to just live with it.

https://tryevercalm.co.uk/pages/evercalm-hand-pain

60-day money-back guarantee. If your hands don't feel like your own again, every penny back.

You've got this.

Tap below now.

And you know what every single one of us told her?

"Your bloods are normal. It's not rheumatoid."

"It's just osteoarthritis. Wear and tear. Normal for your age."

"Take ibuprofen."

"Wear compression gloves."

Then we put her on naproxen. Then Voltarol gel three times a day. Then cortisone injections into her finger joints.

You know what happened?

The naproxen gave her stomach cramps so bad she stopped eating breakfast. The Voltarol wore off in an hour. The cortisone worked for six weeks, then four, then barely two.

And her hands? Still stiff. Still aching. Still getting worse.

The treatments masked the pain. But the joints kept degrading. The stiffness kept spreading. The life kept shrinking.

He didn't need to ask what was wrong.

"It'll take thirty minutes."

"But it'll completely change the way you understand hand and finger pain."

He pulled out a notepad.

Joint degeneration is a symptom, NOT the root cause.

I stared at the words.

Mask the pain with anti-inflammatories.

Rub on topical gel.

Squeeze the swelling down with compression gloves.

Inject cortisone into the worst joints.

"The question you should be asking isn't…"

"'How do I stop the pain in the hands?'"

"The real question should be…"

"'Why are the joints in her fingers and wrists breaking down faster than her body can repair them?'"

That sentence hit me like a brick.

Painkillers masked the pain signal.

Voltarol gel temporarily numbed the surface.

Compression gloves squeezed the swelling.

Cortisone injections temporarily suppressed the local inflammation.

Then he drew tiny arrows flooding in around the cartilage.

"This is chronic low-grade inflammation," he said.

"After menopause, a woman's body loses oestrogen."

"Oestrogen is the body's most powerful natural anti-inflammatory."

"Losing it is like removing a brake."

"Without that brake, inflammatory signals begin flooding the joints — especially the small, delicate joints in the hands and fingers."

Then he tapped the drawing.

"The inflammation attacks the cartilage. The cartilage thins. The joints stiffen. The fingers curl. The grip goes. The pain gets worse."

"And every treatment you prescribe treats what happens AFTER the inflammation has already done its damage."

Then he drew a tap above the hand with water pouring down.

"That's like mopping up a flooded floor while the tap is still running."

"You're cleaning up the damage."

"Not turning off what's causing it."

Every patient I'd told to buy compression gloves.

Every patient I'd injected with cortisone.

Every patient I'd told there was nothing more I could do.

I'd been treating the damage after it happened.

I hadn't been helping the body turn down the inflammation that was causing the damage in the first place.

"As women get older — especially after menopause — the inflammation becomes harder for the body to shut off on its own."

"Without oestrogen's protective brake, it accumulates."

"And as the chronic inflammation builds up around the finger joints, the wrists, the surrounding tissue…"

"The joints degrade faster than the body can repair them."

"When you're younger, your body can usually manage the inflammation and maintain the joint."

"But after 50, that balance shifts."

"The inflammation makes the small joints in the hands more vulnerable to breakdown."

"That's why temporarily masking the pain isn't the same as supporting a healthy inflammatory response."

It was the symptom.

"There's a point that runs along the index finger down to the webbing between the thumb. Healers call it the Hegu point. LI-4."

"It's been documented for over four thousand years."

"The Yellow Emperor's texts describe it. Modern acupuncturists still use it. Memorial Sloan Kettering teaches it."

"For four thousand years, stimulating this one point on the hand has been used to help the body calm its own pain and inflammatory signals."

"And here's what makes it so relevant for hand pain specifically."

He tapped the drawing of the hand.

"The Hegu point is ON the hand. The pressure point that helps regulate inflammation sits in the exact same area as the joints that are being damaged by it."

This was the missing piece.

And once you understand what consistent stimulation at this pressure point does…

You may never look at painkillers, compression gloves, and cortisone injections the same way again.

Because this one pressure point helps support healthy circulation through the hands and fingers.

It helps support the body's own pain-regulation pathways.

It helps support a healthier inflammation response — helping the body turn down the chronic inflammatory signals that are driving the joint damage.

And ultimately, it helps support what every painkiller, gel, glove, and injection fails to do — address the inflammation itself, not just the pain it causes.

I'd been treating the damaged joints.

But I hadn't been supporting the system responsible for protecting them.

Every treatment I'd prescribed for twenty-two years worked downstream.

Not one of them addressed the chronic inflammation attacking the joints from the inside.

And here's what made my blood boil.

This pressure point has been documented for four thousand years. Acupuncturists use it every single day. Researchers have studied it in clinical settings across the world.

But the connection between this pressure point, chronic inflammation, and hand pain after menopause was almost never discussed in mainstream medicine.

You wear it on the hand that needs it most. Every day.

And instead of masking the pain signal or numbing the surface or squeezing the swelling or injecting cortisone that wears off in a fortnight…

It helps the body turn down the tap.

And here's what you need to understand about timing.

Chronic inflammation doesn't improve by being ignored.

After menopause, without oestrogen's protective brake, inflammatory signals continue flooding the joints.

And every month you wait is another month where that inflammation continues breaking down the cartilage you have left.

So if your fingers are stiff and curled up every morning…

If you can't open a jar without asking for help…

If you've had to give up knitting or gardening because your hands won't cooperate…

If you're dropping things you used to hold without thinking…

If your doctor has told you it's just something you'll have to live with…

You MUST address the inflammation. Not just mask the pain.

Tap the link below to discover how the EverCalm ring is helping thousands of women support happier, more comfortable hands — without pills, without injections, without being told to just live with it.
